revisions.body: I read this exchange as a test of the word “all,” not as an admission that pleasures themselves oppose one another. Socrates places pleasures beside opposed states; Protarchus keeps the opposition in their sources while defending the sameness of pleasure as pleasure. That distinction sharpens the challenge: can one name cover experiences arising from unlike conditions without erasing the differences that prompted the inquiry?

The passage first asks us to treat pleasure and intelligence alike as unities with internal kinds. But before that classification is carried out, Socrates recalls a different possibility: neither may be the good, if a third thing proves better than both. What should we make of this change in the task—is the one-and-many inquiry still required for both, or has the conditional claim altered what must be decided first?

revisions.title: Testing sufficiency and giving the mixed life a shape
revisions.body: At this point, the dialogue treats the good as complete and sufficient, then asks whether pleasure or intelligence can stand alone without the other. The accepted record presents this as a test, not yet a completed demonstration. One way to hear the later turn toward kinds is as an attempt to apply the earlier one-and-many method to the mixed life, giving that candidate more structure than a bare preference.

The criterion is deliberately austere: if pleasure or intelligence were the good, neither could need anything further. Socrates therefore examines the two lives separately instead of allowing either to borrow the other’s resources. The accepted record marks this as a setup for examination, not a completed verdict. I hear the next methodological shift through the earlier one-and-many rule: the question becomes how a candidate is one and many, not simply which candidate wins.

revisions.title: Classification becomes a test
revisions.body: At 27e, Philebus places pleasure and pain among things admitting more and less; at 28a, Socrates accepts pleasure’s place in the unlimited genus and turns to wisdom, knowledge, and intellect. My reading is that the pressure of this section comes from that pivot: classification is no longer a neutral inventory, but a question about what kind of thing should lead the argument.

revisions.title: Memory and recollection
revisions.body: This opening makes a distinction the later inquiry can use: memory is described as preserving perception, while recollection is the soul’s recovery, without the body, of what it once underwent with the body. Hear this as a methodological pause: the dialogue is establishing its terms before applying them to desire.

revisions.title: Testing pleasure’s claim to truth
revisions.body: This section puts an earlier question under pressure: can pleasures, like opinions, be true or false? I hear the movement as a warning that pleasure is not judged simply by how strongly it feels. Anticipation, comparison, and escape from pain can make an appearance seem authoritative; the promised discipline is to compare rival accounts rather than let immediacy decide.

revisions.title: Intensity Is Not Yet Value
revisions.body: One way to hear this stretch is as a warning against treating intensity as a verdict. The strongest sensation may be bound to deprivation, pain, or confusion; even laughter can carry an uneasy mixture when it answers another person’s self-misjudgment. I read the passage as leaving us with a sharper question than “Which pleasure is greatest?”: what, exactly, are we learning to praise?

revisions.title: The standard for pure knowledge
revisions.body: At the endpoint of this unit, the inquiry establishes a standard for pure knowledge: what is stable, pure, and unmixed belongs with what remains always the same, while everything else is secondary (claim_philebus_0072). Socrates then gives special honor to nous and phronesis, applying these names to thought about what truly is (claim_philebus_0073; claim_philebus_0074).

revisions.title: From isolated claims to a tested mixture
revisions.body: From the claim that pleasure is the good for every living being, Socrates turns to a test of what a life can actually contain. I read the exchange as rejecting either pleasure or wisdom in isolation and redirecting the inquiry toward their mixture. The important movement is methodological: the mixture is not filled indiscriminately; its contents are admitted cautiously, and the partners must still ask what belongs in it.

revisions.title: Measure before verdict
revisions.body: One way to hear this section is as a search for a standard before a verdict: Protarchus presents intellect as most akin to truth, and contrasts pleasure’s excess with the measure of intellect and knowledge. Read that contrast as the real pressure point. The issue is not simply which feeling wins, but what kind of mixture can remain proportionate enough to count as a good life.

If we hear the closing move as Protarchus—not Socrates—refusing release and promising to recall what remains, what does that make the ending? Against his earlier contrast between intellect’s kinship with truth and pleasure’s lack of measure, does the exchange suggest that inquiry is complete when a comparison is made—or only when its consequences have been carried further?
